# Benchmarks

Current semantic epoch: **rust-native-utf8-v1**. Results from earlier contracts remain in the history and are excluded from these current tables.

Latest results. Execution: ops/s using each workload’s stated operation count. Avg: arithmetic mean of sample rates. Memory: B/KiB/MiB; allocation counts remain counts.

<a id="runtime-int-array-includes"></a>

### int array includes

<details>
<summary>Example and sources (n = 100,000)</summary>

`Build a 129-element int array once per batch. For n queries, use fromIndex = (i * 13 + seed) % 387 - 193, covering both directions, clamping, and beyond-end starts. Values are (position * 37 + seed) % 101, including duplicates; needle is (i * 17 + seed) % 137, including misses. Add one for each includes hit. Start checksum at seed.`

[TSRust source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/int_array_includes.tsr) · [TypeScript source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/int_array_includes.ts) · 3 processes × 31 samples · 8 warmups/process

Dense homogeneous arrays, typed integer offsets, valid Unicode strings, and bounded exact arithmetic. Receiver construction is timed; external input construction and checksum checking are excluded. No coercion, sparse arrays, floating-point NaN, or owned object identity is compared.

</details>

<a id="runtime-fixed-int-array-reverse"></a>

### fixed int array reverse

<details>
<summary>Example and sources (n = 20,000)</summary>

`Construct nine increasing runtime-derived integers per iteration in a fixed array, reverse once in place, then digest every element in its resulting order into a numeric checksum.`

[TSRust source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/fixed_int_array_reverse.tsr) · [TypeScript source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/fixed_int_array_reverse.ts) · 3 processes × 31 samples · 8 warmups/process

Throughput counts completed reversals, one per loop iteration; setup and ordered observation are inside timing. The fixed case keeps its literal local without resizing or escaping, permitting ordinary Rust [i64;9]. The growable case pushes nine values before reversing, so growth/storage costs remain observable. Node uses standard Array.reverse and ignores its return value; no return-identity or allocation-parity claim. Integers and checksum arithmetic are bounded and exact.

</details>

<a id="runtime-int-divide"></a>

### int divide

<details>
<summary>Example and sources (n = 1,000,000)</summary>

`For each iteration form signed numerator -1000..1000 and signed divisor -63..63; replace zero divisor by1. Divide once with truncation toward zero and observe the biased quotient in an ordered digest.`

[TSRust source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/int_divide.tsr) · [TypeScript source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/int_divide.ts) · 3 processes × 31 samples · 8 warmups/process

Operand generation, branching, checked hashing and loop control are timed support costs. Positive input indices and modulo state stay bounded; all integer intermediates are exact in i64 and Number. No failure costs or unchecked overflow are measured. Rust checked integer division versus TS Math.trunc(Number division) is the disclosed contract adapter. Signed zero is not observed by the integer digest. No divide-by-zero or minimum-i64/-1 domain.

</details>

Operand generation, branching, checked hashing and loop control are timed support costs. Positive input indices and modulo state stay bounded; all integer intermediates are exact in i64 and Number. No failure costs or unchecked overflow are measured. Equal, lower and greater cases are checked by an independent arbitrary-integer sign oracle.

</details>

<a id="runtime-number-fixed-local-operations"></a>

### number fixed local operations

<details>
<summary>Example and sources (n = 2,000)</summary>

`One explicitly compound stable local number-array sequence per iteration: write, clone, reverse, full saved/reversed reads, includes and indexOf.`

[TSRust source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/number_fixed_local_operations.tsr) · [TypeScript source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/number_fixed_local_operations.ts) · 3 processes × 31 samples · 8 warmups/process

Whole iteration counts eight-value setup, dynamic indexed write, actual independent scalar clone, reverse, ordered full reads, ordinary0.5 includes and signed-zero indexOf, escaping result retention and loops. No pushes/removes/captures or local storage escape. This is compound operation throughput, not per-instruction latency or total allocation-free execution. JavaScript clone uses actual standard slice for scalar copy. NaN remains in complete retained IEEE output; NaN membership is excluded because JS SameValueZero true differs from native PartialEq false.

</details>

`Initialize a mutable local from bounded runtime-selected operands, execute one actual number compound assignment, and retain every complete primitive result in order. Bitwise and shifts reuse the accepted ToInt32/ToUint32 and count-modulo-32 contracts. No approximate exponentiation or isolated-call claim.

Exact IEEE content and shape observation runs outside timing, preserving signed zero and canonical NaN. Bitwise and shifts reuse the accepted ToInt32/ToUint32 and count-modulo-32 contracts. No approximate exponentiation or isolated-call claim.

<a id="runtime-narrowing-int"></a>

### narrowing int

<details>
<summary>Example and sources (n = 2,048)</summary>

`Three-way payload/null/undefined selection; stable local or direct record field narrowing enables actual arithmetic/valueOf/concat/join/field-read consumers.`

[TSRust source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/narrowing_int.tsr) · [TypeScript source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/narrowing_int.ts) · 3 processes × 31 samples · 8 warmups/process

Full pipeline includes pool or fresh owned payload construction, selection, strict guard evaluation, payload operation and complete output retention; observer outside timing. String concat and Array.join preserve full Unicode content without byte/UTF16 index conversion. Number.valueOf uses existing exact IEEE Number[] observer, including -0; NaN payload identity is not claimed. Record numeric field is copied and String field method borrows it, with no owned subfield consumption. No allocation, owner identity or runtime result claimed.

<a id="runtime-boolean-array-includes"></a>

### boolean array includes

<details>
<summary>Example and sources (n = 100,000)</summary>

`Build a 129-element boolean array once per batch. For n queries, use fromIndex = (i * 13 + seed) % 387 - 193, covering both directions, clamping, and beyond-end starts. Values are (position * 37 + seed) % 101 < 100, with rare false cells; needle alternates by (i + seed) parity. Add one for each includes hit. Start checksum at seed.`

[TSRust source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/boolean_array_includes.tsr) · [TypeScript source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/boolean_array_includes.ts) · 3 processes × 31 samples · 8 warmups/process

Dense homogeneous arrays, typed integer offsets, valid Unicode strings, and bounded exact arithmetic. Receiver construction is timed; external input construction and checksum checking are excluded. No coercion, sparse arrays, floating-point NaN, or owned object identity is compared.

</details>

<a id="runtime-dynamic-unicode-uppercase"></a>

### dynamic unicode uppercase

<details>
<summary>Example and sources (n = 20,000)</summary>

`Retain one real toUpperCase result per iteration from reusable read-only external input containing ASCII, sharp-s/ligature expansion, a combining mark, an astral scalar. Hash every returned scalar in order outside timing.`

[TSRust source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/dynamic_unicode_uppercase.tsr) · [TypeScript source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/dynamic_unicode_uppercase.ts) · 3 processes × 31 samples · 8 warmups/process

Rust str::to_uppercase and Node built-in toUpperCase share the explicitly tested domain: ASCII, ß→SS, ﬀ→FF, ﬁ→FI, ﬂ→FL, é→É, unchanged É/U+0301/U+1F600/NUL. Rust Unicode17 and Node Unicode16 may differ elsewhere; the oracle rejects other mappings and lone surrogates. Input creation is outside timers; actual uppercase construction and retention are inside. Receivers remain read-only without implicit cloning. JavaScript may share immutable strings; no allocation parity or general Unicode-version equivalence is claimed. External argv excludes NUL because operating-system arguments cannot transport it; NUL remains covered by the literal fixture and separate correctness cases.

</details>

<a id="runtime-owned-string-array-reverse"></a>

### owned string array reverse

<details>
<summary>Example and sources (n = 100,000)</summary>

`Construct an owned table once from dynamic input plus É, omega, 😀 and ALPHA. Reverse it in place each iteration, then map every actual value to its content ordinal and digest all positions in order. Observe every reversal, not only final parity.`

[TSRust source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/owned_string_array_reverse.tsr) · [TypeScript source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/owned_string_array_reverse.ts) · 3 processes × 31 samples · 8 warmups/process

Throughput counts one reversal per iteration. Standard case construction and explicit native input cloning occur once inside workload setup. Each reversed position is observed by exact content equality and an ordinal checksum; there is no per-iteration string clone or charAt. This is not a pure reverse microbenchmark: equality/digest observation costs are included. Receivers use native owned strings with reusable borrowed external input. Node ignores reverse return, with no ownership/return-identity equivalence claim. The independent oracle compares scalar sequences, including duplicated input/labels and NUL in separate correctness cases.

</details>

### string last index of default ascii

<details>
<summary>Example and sources (n = 2,048)</summary>

`Find the greatest ascii substring match start at or before the default byte length. Retain every byte index as index + 1, including misses. Empty needles return the selected position; overlapping matches remain visible.`

Needle pool setup, reverse search, selection and complete result retention are timed. ASCII byte offsets equal UTF16 offsets, so the TypeScript counterpart directly calls actual String.lastIndexOf with the same position pool and no coordinate bridge. Complete observation runs outside timing. These are complete iterations, not isolated-call latency or allocation-parity measurements.

</details>

<a id="runtime-string-trim-start-ascii"></a>

### string trim start ascii

<details>
<summary>Example and sources (n = 2,048)</summary>

`Use actual trimStart over eight ascii receiver variants constructed with input clones, one-, two- and three-copy repetition, and literals selected by runtime iteration and seed. Preserve the opposite edge and interior contents, retaining every result in order. The timed whitespace domain is shared by pinned Rust and JavaScript; U+0085 and U+FEFF are excluded.`

[TSRust source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/string_trim_start_ascii.tsr) · [TypeScript source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/string_trim_start_ascii.ts) · 3 processes × 31 samples · 8 warmups/process

Receiver pool setup, runtime selection, trimming and complete output retention are timed; full content observation runs outside timing. Pool setup explicitly clones runtime input twice and constructs one-, two- and three-copy owned repetitions, alongside empty, whitespace-only and padded payload literals. Repeated input preserves interior whitespace. Native Cow literals can retain borrowed static trim slices; owned receivers produce independent owned results. JavaScript may reuse immutable string storage. No isolated-call latency or allocation-parity claim.

</details>

Static quote/template decoding is compile-time work, excluded from runtime-throughput claims. No JS allocation parity or full Number formatting equivalence claim. Measurement pending checkpoint81; no measured result is asserted.

</details>

<a id="runtime-deep-clone"></a>

### deep clone

<details>
<summary>Example and sources (n = 10,000)</summary>

`Each iteration builds nested record with two scores, clones all mutable storage, modifies original score, and sums original and cloned scores plus cloned score count.`

[TSRust source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/deep_clone.tsr) · [TypeScript source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/deep_clone.ts) · 3 processes × 31 samples · 8 warmups/process

Explicit shape-specific deep copy preserves independence of all mutable records/arrays. Both runtimes may share immutable string bytes; mutable records and arrays are copied independently; no allocation parity claim. This is not structuredClone performance. String payloads are carried but their contents are not observed by this numeric checksum; optimizers may eliminate unobservable work. Use ascii_strings for measured and content-validated string transformation.

<a id="runtime-array-some-int"></a>

### array some int

<details>
<summary>Example and sources (n = 2,000)</summary>

`One actual Array.some call per whole iteration over a newly constructed empty or eight-element int receiver, retaining result and exact callback trace/count.`

[TSRust source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/array_some_int.tsr) · [TypeScript source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/array_some_int.ts) · 3 processes × 31 samples · 8 warmups/process

Eleven query modes cover empty, absent, edge, middle, multiple and all-candidate patterns. Actual value eligibility plus index selection determines matches; some/every/findIndex stop forward, findLastIndex walks original indices backward. every uses the complement predicate and stops at a candidate. All callback calls update visible ordered trace and count; the readonly third source parameter supplies length. Whole iteration includes receiver/query setup, typed callback construction/predicate/effects, result retention and loops, not isolated API latency. No output-owner selection, clone or JavaScript alias-identity equivalence is claimed. Domains have different eligibility/support costs and must not be treated as duplicate isolated operations; zero-parameter/factory/invalid semantic cases remain compiler correctness coverage.

</details>

Whole-iteration costs include receiver setup/slice copies, callback construction, value queries/recursive content traversal, capture updates, iteration, and optional unused returned construction/disposal. Native source slices/clone(input) can copy owned contents; readonly JS clone helper is identity. Content/effect equality only, no alias identity equivalence. All actual workload outputs are scalars; observers stay outside the timer.

<a id="runtime-conditional-array-int"></a>

### conditional array int

<details>
<summary>Example and sources (n = 2,048)</summary>

`Evaluate a strict Boolean predicate once and call only the selected same-type branch. Retain every selected payload and complete predicate/left/right call markers in order. Both outcomes and owned sizes0..3 are selected dynamically.`

Whole workload includes setup, selection, per-operation predicate/branch call-counter instrumentation, chosen-branch computation/construction, loop and complete output/counter-marker construction. This is instrumented workload throughput, not pure branch latency. Complete independent observation is outside timing. Fresh owner branches measure selected construction/selection/retention, not existing-owner move cost or JavaScript alias/ownership/allocation parity. 

</details>

<a id="runtime-owned-callbacks"></a>

### owned callbacks

<details>
<summary>Example and sources (n = 10,000)</summary>

`Create counter, move callback through identity and retaining wrapper, invoke twice; then consume a record via a single-use callback returning the entire record and add its seed-valued numeric field.`

[TSRust source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/owned_callbacks.tsr) · [TypeScript source](./benchmarks/runtime/workloads/owned_callbacks.ts) · 3 processes × 31 samples · 8 warmups/process

JS callable references are not ownership transfers; no moved reference is reused. Same call graph, environment state, and record value flow. String payloads are carried but their contents are not observed by this numeric checksum; optimizers may eliminate unobservable work. Use ascii_strings for measured and content-validated string transformation.

</details>
